The first thing my father did after he retired was take the numbers off our house. They were brass, and he wanted to polish them. He set them on newspaper on the kitchen table, where, detached from the brick, they looked less like an address than a disappointing hand of cards: a one, a four, another one. By noon he had made one of the ones shine. By evening he had discovered that the four was not brass at all. Somebody, years before we bought the place, had painted a cheap metal four to match its more distinguished neighbors.

This pleased him enormously. He carried the four around in his shirt pocket for several days, taking it out whenever conversation approached a natural lull. The woman at the pharmacy heard about it. So did a boy collecting money for the school orchestra. My father had spent forty years as a municipal accountant, a profession that had taught him to appreciate discrepancies and had seldom permitted him to enjoy them. Here was a discrepancy with no injured party, no missing receipt, no need for a meeting on Thursday. He stripped the paint and found a handsome gray metal underneath.

My mother wanted the numbers back up. People were beginning to miss the house. A parcel of bath towels went to the neighbors, and a man coming to inspect the furnace drove past twice before calling from the corner. My father agreed that something must be done. What he did was buy a narrow plank of cedar. On this he intended to mount the numbers, setting the gray four a little higher than the brass ones. He showed me a pencil drawing. The effect he was after, he explained, was of a tall child walking between two short parents.

I was thirty-eight then and in a hurry that had already lasted fifteen years. I had come over to borrow a stepladder. Standing in the garage with one hand on its aluminum rail, I suggested that he could simply screw the numbers back into their original holes. He considered this proposal as seriously as he would have considered a revised estimate for resurfacing a road. Then he said, “Well, yes, if the point was to finish.” I laughed because I thought he was making fun of himself. He looked mildly surprised, and I took the ladder home on my car.

For the next month the cedar plank occupied two sawhorses in the garage. My father beveled its edges, disliked the bevel, and made the plank narrower in the course of removing it. He tried three finishes on scraps. When I visited, he was generally sitting on an upturned bucket, studying some part of the operation that did not, to my eye, reward sustained study. Meanwhile my mother wrote 141 on an index card and taped it inside the front window. The card curled in the sun. From the road it resembled a small hand beckoning a driver to come closer.

One Saturday, while we were having coffee, the boy from the orchestra came back. He was selling grapefruit this time. His name was Leon, he played viola, and he wanted to know how the four was coming along. My father took him to the garage. Through the kitchen window I could see them bending over the plank, their heads at nearly the same height because my father had begun to stoop and Leon had not yet begun to grow. My mother bought six grapefruit. “I don’t even like grapefruit,” she said, putting the receipt in the drawer with the scissors.

Leon suggested blue. This was a serious interruption. Until then my father had been working within the range of colors that wood might reasonably be persuaded to become: honey, tobacco, the brown of tea left standing. Blue introduced the question of the front door, which was green, and the shutters, which were black. It also raised the possibility that the plank did not have to look like wood. They spent the afternoon mixing leftover house paint in a yogurt container. At five Leon went home with a blue thumbnail and my father went in to lie down before supper.

The finished sign was nothing special. I think this is important. The blue dried darker than either of them expected. The four, raised half an inch above the ones, looked like a four that somebody had put on crooked. There were two visible screw heads, although my father dabbed them with paint. He installed it crooked, too, then corrected it, leaving a small pale wound in the brick. My mother took down the index card. The furnace man found us on his first try the following autumn, an achievement for which he received considerably more praise than he could understand.

I have the sign now, in a box with a meat thermometer, some photographs, and the key to a car nobody in the family owns. I could put it on my own house, but my number is sixty, and even my father would have admitted that this presents difficulties. Sometimes I take it out when I am looking for something else. The back is more interesting than the front. There are six pencil marks where he considered placing the four. There is a blue whorl left by a thumb. A cedar shaving is caught beneath the head of a screw.

Last week I finally returned the stepladder. Not to my father, of course, but to Leon, who bought the house with his husband and keeps finding things my father left unfinished. We stood in the garage deciding where the ladder ought to go. It would fit beside the door if we moved a hook; it would fit behind the workbench if we shortened a shelf. Leon got a tape measure. His husband brought out three chairs and a plate of sliced pears. After a while we folded the ladder and laid it on the floor, where it was in nobody’s way that afternoon.
